lesson.title: Make it light up
lesson.subtitle: Close the loop, test what conducts, and keep your LED safe

video.title: Make it light up
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Okafor — your science teacher (main character)
Mr Joseph — your computer studies teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talks to the student)

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor at the lab bench beside Amani, a student holding a battery, a torch bulb and a single wire. First try: the bulb stays dark. She shifts the wire and the bulb glows.
scenes.animation: Bulb stays dark, wire slides, bulb lights with a small glow.
scenes.narration: Amani had a battery, a bulb and one wire. She tried to light the bulb: nothing. Then she moved the wire, and it lit! What changed? Let's find out.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: build a circuit that lights up, and keep it safe.

scenes.visual: A battery, a wire and a torch bulb drawn large; dots flow out of the battery, in at the bulb's tip, out at its metal side and back. Then the first try: the wire on the tip only, and the dots stop.
scenes.animation: Dots circulate; the contacts glow in turn; the loop breaks and the dots halt.
scenes.on_screen_text: A circuit is a closed loop
scenes.narration: A circuit is a loop: current flows out of the battery, through the bulb, and back in. A bulb has two contacts, its tip and its side, and the loop must pass through both. Amani's first try touched only one.

scenes.visual: A bicycle seen from the side: the pedals turn, the chain runs round, the back wheel spins. A link snaps and everything stops.
scenes.animation: Chain runs; a link pops open; the wheel slows to a stop.
scenes.narration: Think of a bicycle chain. The pedals push, like the battery. The moving chain is the current, and the back wheel is the bulb. Break the chain anywhere, and everything stops.

scenes.visual: A tester with two free wire ends. Objects slide under the ends one by one: a coin, a key, foil and a pencil light the bulb; a ruler, an eraser, paper and a stick don't.
scenes.animation: Each object drops into its column as the bulb lights or stays dark.
scenes.narration: To test a material, leave a gap in your loop and let both ends touch it. If the bulb lights, it's a conductor: coins, keys, foil, pencil lead. If not, it's an insulator: plastic, rubber, paper, dry wood.

scenes.visual: Amina beside Kofi's circuit; a magnifier shows one wire end still covered in plastic. Two answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Kofi's wires both touch the bulb, but one end is still inside its plastic coat. Will the bulb light?

scenes.visual: The covered end stays dark; then a stripped end shows bright copper and the bulb glows. A cut-away wire shows copper inside plastic.
scenes.animation: Plastic slides back; copper touches; glow.
scenes.narration: No. Plastic is an insulator, so the loop is still open. Strip the end, and the copper closes it. That's why wires are copper inside plastic.

scenes.visual: A big red LED with a long and a short leg; a plus sign by the long one. It flips round and goes dark, flips back and lights.
scenes.animation: The LED flips, goes dark, flips back and glows.
scenes.on_screen_text: An LED works one way round
scenes.narration: Now swap the bulb for an LED, the light in phone screens and solar lamps. It works only one way round: long leg to plus. Backwards, it stays dark.

scenes.visual: An LED straight on a battery flashes and goes black. Then a small striped resistor slides into the loop and a new LED glows steadily; a bicycle brake squeezes the chain gently.
scenes.animation: Flash and smoke; resistor slides in; steady glow.
scenes.narration: But an LED can't limit its own current. Straight on a battery, too much flows, and it burns out. A resistor in the loop holds the current down, like a gentle brake on the chain.

scenes.visual: Two AA batteries, a resistor and a red LED in a loop; the sum writes itself on a board beside them.
scenes.animation: Each line of the sum writes in as it is said; the LED glows at the end.
scenes.narration: How big a resistor? Two AA batteries give three volts; a red LED uses about two, leaving one. For a safe ten milliamps, that volt needs a hundred ohms. A bigger resistor gives a dimmer LED.

scenes.visual: A bare wire laid straight across a battery glows red; a hand pulls back. A wall socket with a big cross.
scenes.animation: The wire reddens; the socket gets a cross badge.
scenes.narration: Never make a short circuit: a wire straight from plus to minus. A huge current flows, and the wire and battery get hot enough to burn. And use batteries only: a wall socket can kill.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph beside Musa, who holds a bare wire towards both ends of a battery. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Musa holds a bare wire straight across his battery, to test it. No bulb. What happens?

scenes.visual: Four icons line up: a loop, a coin and a ruler, an LED, a resistor.
scenes.narration: They get hot: that's a short circuit, so never do it. Remember: close the loop, test what conducts, long leg to plus, and always a resistor.

scenes.visual: A student's desk at home: two AA batteries taped together, a torch bulb, foil strips, and ten small objects in a row; a notebook with two columns.
scenes.animation: The bulb lights for the coin, stays dark for the ruler; ticks appear in the notebook.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: make a tester from two AA batteries, a torch bulb and kitchen foil. Predict, then test ten things at home or at school, and sort them into two lists. Next time, switches that decide.

checkpoints.prompt: Both wires touch the bulb, but one wire's end is still inside its plastic coat. Will the bulb light?

options.text: No: the plastic keeps the loop open

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — plastic is an insulator, so the loop stays open and no current flows.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the plastic coat is an insulator. The copper never touches, so the loop stays open and the bulb stays dark.

checkpoints.prompt: Musa holds a bare wire straight across his battery. There's no bulb. What happens?

options.text: The wire and battery get hot
Nothing: there's no bulb to light

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — that's a short circuit. Almost nothing limits the current, so the wire and battery heat up fast.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — with nothing in the loop to limit it, a huge current flows. That's a short circuit, and the wire gets hot enough to burn.
